newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Heineken not giving up on Israel's Tempo.
newsitem.headline: Heineken not giving up on Israel's Tempo.

text.p: Dutch brewer Heineken NV is still interested in Israel's Tempo Beer Industries although an option to acquire a controlling stake expired on May 3, a spokeswoman said on Wednesday.
"Negotiations are still going on and we are still interested," Heineken spokeswoman Margritha Meijer told Reuters.
She said Heineken executives would be coming to Israel in the next few days but could offer no details on further talks.

Moshe Podhorzer, who controls 44.5 percent of Tempo, said on Tuesday that he would not extend the option he granted to majority shareholder Jack Bar. The option had given Bar 90 days to reach an accord with Heineken that would enable the Dutch brewer to buy at least 51 percent of Tempo.
Podhorzer termed the decision "final" but indicated in a statement that he would be prepared to consider a new option offer on different terms.

"Representatives of Heineken's management told him (Monday) night that they would be arriving in the country in the next few days for a series of meetings....If negotiations are renewed, they will not be on the current terms and framework," a statement from Podhorzer's spokesman said.

Tempo is Israel's largest brewer, producing products under its own label and Heineken beer under license. It is also the Israeli bottler for Pepsi Cola, but its soft drinks business has performed poorly in recent years.
Tempo's beer business accounts for 60 to 70 percent of revenues, industry sources estimate.

The 90-day option entitled Bar, who together with allied shareholders controls 51 percent of Tempo, to acquire the Pordhorzer group's stake for $42 million. The new shareholders were then planning to split Tempo into two publicly traded companies for beer and soft drinks, with Heineken retaining a holding only in the brewing business.

Newspaper reports have said Heineken would buy into Tempo at a lower valuation than the Bar group would be paying. However, buying out Podhorzer would end years of infighting between the rival shareholder groups that has hurt Tempo's business, industry observers said.
Meijer would not say why Heineken had not reached an agreement within the 90-day period. "It's a complex situation. We needed more time," she said.
Podhorzer said Tempo should use its internal resources to the best of its ability "without an international strategic partner, although this is always a good business option."
